documents.title: Academic Integrity and Syllabus Support in the Age of Generative AI
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors to write their own explicit AI policy and offers sample statements and templates that range from permissive to a ban ('Using AI tools to generate any work is considered plagiarism'). It sets no school-wide rule, so the decision sits with each instructor and assignment.
documents.summary: Steinhardt's AI Hub page guides faculty on writing syllabus AI policies, with many sample statements for writing, art and music, advice on discussions, privacy, assessment design, citation and detection. It sets no single rule and leaves permission to instructors.

units.why: Opening framing: policies 'should outline when and how AI tools ... can be used'. A recommendation to instructors to set explicit use rules, so it is a syllabus-statement requirement (P09) rather than a stance.
units.anchor: These policies should outline when and how AI tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity.ai
units.frag_start: These policies should outline
units.frag_end: ethical implications of AI in academic work

units.why: The page points faculty to a chatbot that drafts sample syllabus statements; 'check out this AI Chatbot we created' is a school-provided tool supporting instructors, which fits P63 (support faculty) better than P17 (a student-facing tool).
units.anchor: check out this AI Chatbot we created
units.frag_start: If you're interested, check out
units.policy: The school offers an AI chatbot that gives instructors sample syllabus statements based on their course information and preferences.
units.fit_note: The tool drafts syllabus statements; it supports instructors with AI itself rather than workshops.

units.why: 'Clearly define what AI tools can be used for in your course' tells instructors to set permitted uses, with examples such as brainstorming and drafting. Allocates the decision to each instructor, P04.
units.anchor: Clearly define what AI tools can be used for in your course
units.frag_start: Clearly define what AI tools
units.policy: Instructors clearly define what AI tools can be used for in their course (e.g., brainstorming, idea generation, or drafting) and where they are prohibited (e.g., completing graded assignments without supervision).

units.why: Sample statement permitting AI for 'initial idea generation and draft creation' while final work stays the student's; brainstorming is the closest fit (P15), with the originality condition noted.
units.anchor: may use AI tools like ChatGPT for initial idea generation and draft creation
units.frag_start: Students may use AI tools
units.policy: Students may use AI tools like ChatGPT for initial idea generation and draft creation, but final submissions must reflect the student's original thoughts and revisions.
units.fit_note: Also covers drafting and requires final submissions to reflect the student's original thoughts.

units.why: Under 'Prohibited Use Cases', instructors should 'establish boundaries' such as no AI-generated full essays or homework solutions. Nearest type is P19 (AI may not produce submitted work).
units.anchor: using AI to generate full essays or solutions to homework problems
units.frag_start: Establish boundaries for AI use
units.policy: Instructors establish boundaries for AI use to prevent academic misconduct, such as using AI to generate full essays or solutions to homework problems.
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors as guidance for drawing boundaries, not a direct student ban.

units.why: Example statement classes any AI-generated work as plagiarism with 'disciplinary action'. This is a sample blanket ban; P36 (misconduct classification) is chosen because the statement's core is plagiarism and discipline, though it also acts as a P01 ban.
units.anchor: generate any work is considered plagiarism and will result in disciplinary action
units.frag_start: Using AI tools to generate any work
units.fit_note: Sample statement also bans all AI-generated work, as a P01 default ban would.

units.why: Under 'Ethical AI Use' instructors should include 'proper attribution when AI-generated content is used'; a disclosure expectation (P24).
units.anchor: proper attribution when AI-generated content is used in assignments
units.frag_start: Include guidelines on ethical AI usage
units.policy: Instructors include guidelines on ethical AI usage, including proper attribution when AI-generated content is used in assignments.

units.why: Sample statement: AI content 'must be properly attributed' and failure to disclose 'may result in plagiarism charges', making nondisclosure the violation (P28).
units.anchor: Failure to disclose AI assistance may result in plagiarism charges.
units.frag_start: Any AI-generated content used in assignments

units.why: Introduces templates that instructors adapt so students know 'when AI can be used and how to properly acknowledge' it. A supply of template language for syllabi, P09.
units.anchor: these templates ensure students are fully informed about when AI can be used
units.frag_start: These templates ensure students
units.policy: The templates ensure students are fully informed about when AI can be used and how to properly acknowledge AI-generated content.

units.why: 'you can establish different AI policies for each assignment' and communicate the decision clearly: per-assignment rules, P04.
units.anchor: you can establish different AI policies for each assignment
units.frag_start: you can establish different AI policies
units.frag_end: clearly communicate this decision to your students.
units.policy: Instructors can establish different AI policies for each assignment and must clearly communicate this decision to students.
units.fit_note: Also asks that the per-assignment decision be clearly communicated.

units.why: General template permits AI 'for brainstorming or refining ideas' while 'all work submitted must be your own'; brainstorming type P15 with ownership condition.

documents.title: Using Generative AI: Generative AI and Academic Integrity
documents.stance_why: The guide says AI use 'is not cheating if a faculty member approves its use in a class assignment' and that unapproved use risks violating the Academic Integrity Policy, so each class sets the rule rather than the guide.
documents.summary: A Libraries research guide explains how NYU's Academic Integrity Policy applies to AI, lists NYU-provided AI tools, notes that Turnitin AI detection is disabled, and gives advice on evaluating and citing AI output. It defers AI permission to faculty.

units.why: Library guide opens by saying AI use 'is not cheating if a faculty member approves its use'; approval per class sets the rule, P04.
units.anchor: Using Generative AI tools is not cheating if a faculty member approves its use
units.frag_start: Using Generative AI tools is not cheating

units.why: 'if these tools have not been approved, students run the risk of violating NYU's Academic Integrity Policy' gives the fallback when unapproved: P06.
units.anchor: if these tools have not been approved, students run the risk of violating
units.frag_start: if these tools have not been approved

units.why: Quotes the policy defining cheating as 'submitting work ... that was created by another, substantially or in whole, as one's own'; the integrity rule applied to AI, P19.
units.anchor: that was created by another, substantially or in whole, as one's own
units.frag_start: submitting work (papers, homework assignments
units.fit_note: Policy text names 'another' rather than AI; the guide applies it to AI tools.

units.why: Quoted definition includes 'bringing or accessing unauthorized materials during an examination'; exams, P22.
units.anchor: bringing or accessing unauthorized materials during an examination
units.frag_start: bringing or accessing unauthorized materials
units.fit_note: General unauthorized-materials rule, applied to technology generally.

units.why: Integrity is violated by 'any behavior that violates the academic policies set forth by the student's NYU School, department, or division', so unit rules bind; P36.
units.anchor: any behavior that violates the academic policies set forth by the student
units.frag_start: any behavior that violates the academic policies

units.why: 'it is important for students and faculty to clarify the extent of the use of AI tools in specific classes and assignments': P10 is the closest fit for students seeking clarity.
units.anchor: clarify the extent of the use of AI tools in specific classes and assignments
units.frag_start: it is important for students and faculty to clarify
units.fit_note: Addressed to both students and faculty, not only students asking first.

units.why: The guide lists institutional Gemini, NotebookLM and Microsoft Copilot accessed with NetID; a sanctioned university AI tool, P17.

units.policy: NYU offers Generative AI services for student, staff, and faculty use, including institutional instances of Gemini, NotebookLM and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

units.frag_start: In most cases, AI writing tools should not be used

units.policy: In general, acknowledgements of AI tools include the tool name, prompt, platform name, platform version, and date the output was generated.

notes: NYU university-level pages on www.nyu.edu were inaccessible (bot challenge), so the university layer is only the Libraries guide. No computing-unit policy found. Steinhardt is a school of education, not computing.
